actions: initiates/assists glenohumeral abduction (first ~15deg, then throughout with deltoid)
stabilizes humeral head in glenoid (rotator cuff force-couple)

functional_compartments.name: Anterior compartment (larger, more pennate)

neuromuscular_junction_zone.location_description: central tendon endplate band, short highly-pennate fascicles

functional_compartments.function_note: Larger anterior compartment generates most of the abduction-initiation torque; documented as mechanically/architecturally distinct from the posterior compartment.
functional_compartments.source: Roh MS et al. (2000) Clin Orthop Relat Res 375:242-249 (supraspinatus anterior/posterior compartmentalization); Kim SY et al. cadaveric partition studies

functional_compartments.name: Posterior compartment (smaller)
functional_compartments.function_note: Smaller posterior compartment; contributes proportionally less PCSA.
functional_compartments.source: Roh MS et al. (2000) Clin Orthop Relat Res 375:242-249

trigger_points.location_description: Medial belly point, in the mid-fossa of the supraspinous fossa, deep to trapezius
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Deep ache in the mid-deltoid region, spreading down the lateral arm and forearm and often concentrating at the lateral epicondyle; occasionally to the wrist.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Felt during abduction and when carrying weights at the side; may produce a dull ache at rest.
trigger_points.notes: One of two classic belly points described for this muscle (with the lateral belly point below); an occasional third tender point is described near the musculotendinous/tendon zone at the greater tuberosity, without a separately characterised referral pattern.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons Trigger Point Manual -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (Donnelly JM, Fernandez-de-las-Penas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds), Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual, 3rd ed., Wolters Kluwer, 2019)

trigger_points.location_description: Lateral belly point, just medial to the acromion, deep to trapezius
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Deep ache in the mid-deltoid region, spreading down the lateral arm and forearm and often concentrating at the lateral epicondyle; occasionally to the wrist.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Felt during abduction and when carrying weights at the side; may produce a dull ache at rest.
trigger_points.notes: Second of the two classic belly points (with the medial belly point above).

clinical.function_biomechanics: Initiates and assists glenohumeral abduction throughout the range and compresses the humeral head into the glenoid (concavity compression). Contrary to the old “first 15° only” teaching, selective-block dynamometry shows supraspinatus and deltoid contribute roughly equal torque across the functional planes of elevation. Contributes ~14% of total cuff moment (deltoid-independent). Minor: slight external rotation with the arm at the side; anterior fibres tension the rotator cable.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: Subacromial–subdeltoid bursa directly above the tendon (separates it from the acromion, coracoacromial ligament and deltoid); normally does not communicate with the glenohumeral joint — communication implies a full-thickness cuff tear. Adjacent structures — mutual influence: Coracoacromial arch (acromion, CA ligament, AC joint) above — the classic site of subacromial impingement and of extrinsic tendon compression; AC-joint osteophytes and os acromiale narrow the outlet. Suprascapular nerve at the notch — entrapment weakens supraspinatus + infraspinatus. Long head of biceps runs just anterior at the rotator interval. Tears allow superior humeral-head migration, secondarily loading the acromion and biceps.

trigger_points.location: Two belly TrPs (deep to trapezius): a medial point in the mid-fossa and a lateral point just medial to the acromion; occasionally a tender point at the musculotendinous/tendon zone near the greater tuberosity.
trigger_points.referred_pain: Deep ache in the mid-deltoid region, spreading down the lateral arm and forearm and often concentrating at the lateral epicondyle; occasionally to the wrist. Felt during abduction and when carrying weights at the side; may produce a dull ache at rest.
trigger_points.source: Donnelly JM, Fernández-de-las-Peñas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds). Travell, Simons & Simons’ Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual. 3rd ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2019. Muscle chapters as named in each section.

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: Into this territory (suprascapular/lateral shoulder): upper trapezius TrP3, levator scapulae, infraspinatus (rarely), scaleni
AC-joint irritation refers to the trapezius–supraspinatus region
C4–C5/C5–C6 facet pain maps over the suprascapular fossa and shoulder
C5 radiculopathy and neuralgic amyotrophy present as deep shoulder-girdle pain here.
clinical.movement_restrictions_aggravators: Painful arc/limited active abduction, pain reaching overhead or backwards (combing hair, reaching a back pocket), night ache lying on the shoulder; carrying bags at the side aggravates.
clinical.notes: Most-torn cuff tendon by convention, though the footprint work shows many “supraspinatus” tears involve infraspinatus; check spinati atrophy (suprascapular neuropathy, C5–C6 root, neuralgic amyotrophy) before attributing weakness to the tendon.
clinical.caveat: Trigger-point locations and referral maps derive from the Travell–Simons clinical-observational tradition, now standardised by Delphi consensus criteria [32] and supported by prevalence and hyperalgesia studies in shoulder pain [30,31]; they are expert-level evidence, not trial-level, and inter-examiner reliability of TrP palpation is moderate. Facet, ACJ and subacromial referral patterns, by contrast, come from experimental provocation in volunteers/patients [33,34,37]. Textbook anatomy is cited at section level; where major texts disagree (segmental levels), the range is given and flagged. Figures and patterns older than 12 months are anatomical/physiological constants and are not considered stale.
